problem:
Meridian Bank offers instant cross-border payments from Europe to a customer in India. A corporate customer, Aldergrove Manufacturing, pays a supplier in India and expects the payment to arrive instantly, because the euro leg is instant. The payment is accepted, the euro leg completes in seconds, and then nothing happens for hours. The supplier has not been credited, the customer asks where the money is, and the support team cannot answer, because it has been treating the payment as one instant payment rather than as two legs with different rules.

The distinction is the EPC One-Leg-Out Instant Credit Transfer, or OCT Inst. It covers the euro leg of a cross-border instant payment where one leg sits outside SEPA. The Rulebook 2025 version 1.1 is effective 5 October 2025. The euro leg follows the instant euro rules, including the 10-second execution maximum and Verification of Payee where it applies. The non-euro leg follows the destination corridor's own rules, its own timing, its own settlement arrangement and its own confirmation, and it is not instant simply because the euro leg is. The customer promise must be built from the slower leg, and the end-to-end state must be reported only when the required leg confirmations are received.

Meridian Bank needs an orchestration model that treats each leg separately, with its own state, timeout and confirmation, and that reports the overall outcome honestly: the euro leg complete, the non-euro leg pending, or the payment failed with a defined compensation. The bank must not report end-to-end completion until the required confirmations arrive, and it must not resubmit blindly when a leg times out.
solution:
Model the payment as an orchestration with two legs, not as a single instant payment. The euro leg is covered by OCT Inst under Rulebook 2025 version 1.1, effective 5 October 2025, and it follows the instant euro rules, including the 10-second execution maximum. The non-euro leg follows the destination corridor's own rules, its own timing, its own settlement arrangement and its own confirmation. Each leg gets its own state machine, its own timeout and its own confirmation, and the overall orchestration state is reported only from the leg states, never assumed.

Define the customer promise from the slower leg. The customer must be told that the euro leg can complete in seconds while the destination credit follows the corridor's timing, and the status shown to the customer must name each leg's state, so a payment with a complete euro leg and a pending non-euro leg is shown exactly that way. End-to-end completion is reported only when the required leg confirmations are received. If a leg times out, the payment enters an unknown or investigation state, and it is not blindly resubmitted. Compensation or return follows the defined scheme and corridor rules, with exactly-once financial effect enforced by unique financial event IDs.

Keep the cover and customer legs correlated but distinct. The pacs.009 cover leg and the pacs.008 customer leg can have different states, so a cover return must trigger an investigation of both legs before any customer adjustment is posted. Use the UETR and the end-to-end reference to link the legs across the corridor, and reconcile each leg separately against its own settlement report. Test the orchestration with the hard cases: destination timeout, late success after timeout, cover return with an unclear customer leg, and duplicate callbacks, and prove that each resolves to exactly one financial effect.

decision.question: You are the business analyst for Meridian Bank. A corporate customer pays a supplier in India and expects the payment to arrive instantly because the euro leg is instant. The euro leg completes in seconds, the supplier has not been credited hours later, and support cannot explain where the money is. What model do you recommend?

options.label: A
options.detail: Resubmit the payment immediately so the supplier is credited faster.

options.label: B
options.detail: Refund the sender at once and cancel the payment.

options.label: C
options.detail: Model each leg separately with its own state, timeout and confirmation, and report the true end-to-end state, including that the euro leg is complete and the non-euro leg is pending.

options.label: D
options.detail: Tell the customer the payment is complete because the euro leg finished in seconds.

decisionRationale: Option C is correct because OCT Inst covers only the euro leg, and the non-euro leg follows the destination corridor's own rules and timing, so each leg needs its own state, timeout and confirmation. Option D misleads the customer about a payment that has not completed end to end. Option A risks a duplicate payment. Option B refunds a payment that may still complete.

happy: The payment is split into its euro and non-euro legs under one orchestration reference. The euro leg executes under OCT Inst within the 10-second maximum, the non-euro leg completes under the corridor arrangement, and end-to-end completion is reported only when both required confirmations are received. The customer sees the true state at each stage, and the ledger reconciles leg by leg.

negative.title: Destination timeout
negative.detail: The non-euro leg is sent but the destination system does not confirm beneficiary credit within the timeout. Keep the payment in an unknown or investigation state, do not resubmit blindly, and trigger the defined investigation or compensation process only under the agreed rules.

negative.title: Sender debited but no beneficiary credit
negative.detail: The sender's account is debited and the receiving system reports a technical failure or no final response. Establish whether the debit is provisional, final or held, then apply the scheme and corridor rules to decide whether to await confirmation, return funds or investigate, with exactly one financial effect.

negative.title: Late success after timeout
negative.detail: A success confirmation arrives after the timeout and after a compensation has been started. Resolve the race using the leg state and the unique financial event ID, so the beneficiary is credited once and the sender is not also refunded for the same payment.

negative.title: Cover returned while customer leg unclear
negative.detail: The cover leg is returned but the underlying customer credit transfer has a different state. Correlate the cover and the customer payment by stable references, determine the customer leg's state first, and do not assume the cover return defines the customer outcome.

negative.title: Duplicate callback
negative.detail: The destination system sends the same confirmation twice. Do not resubmit. Use the original idempotency key and correlation ID to check the existing state, and only a governed replay under the defined rules may re-send a leg.

technical: Model the payment as an orchestration with a leg-level state machine for the euro leg and the non-euro leg, plus an overall orchestration state derived from the legs. Use a single end-to-end reference and UETR where applicable across both legs, with separate leg identifiers for tracing. Apply the OCT Inst rules to the euro leg only, including the 10-second execution budget, and apply the corridor rules to the non-euro leg. Use idempotency keys per leg so a retry or a duplicate callback cannot create a second financial effect, and use unique financial event IDs for every debit, credit, compensation and return. Keep a durable event store of leg states, timeouts and confirmations, and design the investigation view to show both legs and the orchestration state on one screen.

accounting: The euro leg and the non-euro leg settle under different arrangements, so each leg has its own liquidity, settlement and reconciliation treatment. The euro leg settles through the instant euro infrastructure, while the non-euro leg settles under the corridor's own arrangement, and the overall customer transaction reconciles only when both legs are confirmed or when the defined compensation has been applied. Operations works from a leg-level worklist that shows each leg's state and age, and Treasury must hold liquidity for the euro leg and manage the foreign exchange and settlement risk on the non-euro leg. A failed non-euro leg after a successful euro leg creates a defined compensation or return obligation, and the accounting must show the compensation as a separate linked event, never as a silent reversal of the euro leg.
